Chaos in the EGX30? A replication of Morad, Rady & Amin (2019)

Replication, referee-requested revisions, and a validated chaos toolkit

Published

September 25, 2026

Summary of findings

Bottom line. The EGX30 data reproduce the paper’s descriptive results closely. Every test that can separate chaos from noise, once validated, rejects low-dimensional chaos. The nonlinearity the paper found is volatility clustering plus regime shifts in volatility. The long-memory and 1,240-day-cycle claims do not survive bias correction and correct critical values. This supports the referee’s recommendation to recast the paper as a study of nonlinearity and weak-form efficiency.

Validation (Section 2) shows which tools can be trusted.

  • DChaos λ̂ discriminates. It recovers λ = 0.693 on the logistic map (λ̂ = 0.678). It stays positive and non-rejected with measurement noise, and is significantly negative for GARCH, IID and fGn. In the Monte Carlo it calls chaos in 0% of GARCH and IID replications and 100% of noisy-logistic ones.
  • DChaos fails on the periodic map. On the period-4 map (r = 3.5) it reports λ̂ = 0.260 without rejecting chaos. The neural-net estimator breaks down on a degenerate 4-point orbit, so λ̂ is never read alone. The 0–1 test gets that case right (K ≈ 0).
  • Nearest-neighbour forecasts discriminate. They beat the mean forecast only for deterministic data.
  • The 0–1 test cannot tell noise from chaos. It gives K ≈ 1 for GARCH and IID noise in 100% of replications. It only separates regular from irregular dynamics, so K ≈ 1 on EGX30 is uninformative.
  • Raw BDS cannot tell GARCH from chaos. It rejects IID in 100% of GARCH replications and in 0% once GARCH-filtered.
  • AMI does not pick the right delay for maps. It picks τ = 3–7 for the logistic map, whose delay is 1, so all embeddings use τ = 1.
  • Classical R/S is biased upward. It gives H ≈ 0.55 on IID noise; the Anis–Lloyd–Peters correction brings it to 0.49.

Replication, paper window 2000–2015.

  • Table 1. Mean, sd, skewness, kurtosis and IQR match the paper to two or three significant digits. The file lacks 1998–1999, so N = 3,894 rather than 4,393.
  • Table 2. ADF and PP statistics match in sign and scale. BIC selects AR(1) and AIC selects AR(10); AR(2) residuals fail Ljung–Box.
  • Table 3 (referee M3 confirmed). The paper’s variance ratios are those of the differenced returns: 0.603, 0.300, 0.156, 0.076 here against 0.608, 0.304, 0.158, 0.077 printed. Computed correctly, VR(2) = 1.181 (> 1), with robust z₂ = 5.5. The random walk is rejected because of positive autocorrelation, the opposite of what the paper’s Table 3 implies.
  • Table 4. BDS on raw and AR(2)-filtered returns is huge (W = 13–29). The AR(2) filter barely changes it, confirming the rejection is not linear.
  • Tables 5–6 (referee M5 confirmed). No sub-period length in the paper’s grid divides N. With the corrected H and 2,000 shuffles, only the full 10–1,240 range is significant (one-sided p = 0.022), and the corrected H is only 0.537. Over 350–700, H = 0.44, which is below 0.5 and contradicts the paper.
  • Table 7 (referee M6 confirmed). With Lo’s correct 95% region [0.809, 1.862], V exceeds the bound only for q ≤ 16. It never exceeds the 99% bound, and it falls to 1.48–1.76 once q ≥ N^½. That is short-range dependence, not long memory.

Referee revisions.

  • M2: GARCH-filtered BDS.
    • Filtering removes almost all of the rejection. After AR(2)-GJR-t filtering, BDS falls from W ≈ 16–29 to |W| ≤ 1.82 (2000–2015) and ≤ 2.41 (2000–2025).
    • Asymptotic p-values. No asymptotic rejection at 5% in 2000–2015; a few at large ε in 2000–2025.
    • Parametric bootstrap. The bootstrap (199 refits) bands are narrower than N(0,1) at large m and ε. It therefore flags remaining dependence at ε ≥ 1.5 sd and m ≥ 3, where the ARCH-LM test also shows residual ARCH (p ≈ 0.02). That points to a misspecified variance, not to chaos.
    • Leverage. EGARCH finds a significant leverage term; GJR does not in the full sample.
  • M1: chaos diagnostics on AR(2) and GJR-t residuals, both samples.
    • Lyapunov exponent. λ̂ ranges from -2.84 to -0.60. It is negative, and H₀: λ ≥ 0 is rejected in every case.
    • Correlation dimension. It does not saturate; it grows with m like IID noise.
    • Cao’s method. It finds no embedding dimension.
    • Nearest-neighbour forecasts. Out-of-sample MSE is 7–11% worse than the mean forecast.
  • M4: long memory. Local-Whittle d is 0.071 (se 0.034) for 2000–2015. The larger GPH estimates use m = √N and pick up the short-range AR component.
  • M7: breaks and regimes.
    • Break tests agree. strucchange, ecp and PELT locate breaks around the 2003 pound float, the 2008 crisis, 2011–12 and the 2020 COVID shock.
    • Regime-switching volatility fits better. MS-GJR-t beats single-regime GJR-t by BIC, with daily volatilities of 1.14% and 1.98% and very persistent regimes. TV-GARCH detects a shift in unconditional variance.
  • M8: subsamples. λ̂ is negative in every subsample, before and after the November 2016 float, and dropping the 2011 closure return changes nothing. The magnitude of λ̂ is unstable across subsamples (the neural-net estimator is noisy); its sign is not.

1 Data

The supplied file data/raw/egx30_2000_2025.csv holds daily EGX30 closes. The paper used January 1998 – December 2015 (N = 4,393 returns). The file starts on 2 January 2000, so the paper window here is 2000–2015 (N = 3894). The difference of 499 returns is almost exactly two trading years (1998–1999), so the paper’s N is consistent with this source.

2 Validating the toolkit

Before any test is applied to EGX30 it is run on series with known dynamics: the logistic map at r = 4 (chaotic, λ = ln 2 = 0.693), the same map with measurement noise (sd 0.05), the logistic map at r = 3.5 (periodic), GARCH(1,1)-t and AR(1)-GJR-GARCH-t noise (stochastic, non-IID, not chaotic), IID Gaussian noise, and fractional Gaussian noise with H = 0.7 (long memory). All series have n = 3,000.

Column key: bds_* are BDS W at m = 2, ε = 1 sd, on the raw series and on GARCH(1,1) standardized residuals. H_AL is the Anis–Lloyd–Peters corrected Hurst exponent and lw_d the local-Whittle d. tau_ami is the AMI first-minimum delay, reported only. cao_m is Cao’s embedding dimension (NA means no saturation). D2_m* is the correlation dimension. K01 is the 0–1 test. nn_* is the nearest-neighbour forecast MSE relative to the mean, with its Diebold–Mariano p-value. lle and lle_p_H0_chaos are the DChaos neural-network largest Lyapunov exponent and the p-value for H₀: λ ≥ 0.

4.5 Structural breaks and regimes (M7–M8)

Bai–Perron (strucchange, weekly returns, BIC). Mean breaks: 2003-03-19, 2006-01-29. Volatility breaks: 2008-08-07, 2009-11-18. The sup-F test for a single mean break has p = 0.045.

E-divisive (ecp, weekly returns) distributional change points: 2003-03-19, 2008-05-06, 2009-02-08.

5 Reproducibility

  • Pipeline: targets (_targets.R), with functions in R/. Packages are pinned in renv.lock, and report.qmd is rendered by tar_quarto().
  • Seeds are fixed in tar_option_set(seed = ...) and in each bootstrap.
  • Critical values: Lo (1991) Table II. BDS uses ε in units of the series sd.
  • Key settings: DChaos uses the QR (SLE) method with bootstrap blocking, m ∈ 1–4, h ∈ 2–10, and B = 500. BDS parametric bootstrap uses B = 199. The Hurst bootstrap uses B = 2,000.
